source_records.abstract: Background: Antimicrobial agents have transformed the management of infectious diseases and remain among the most frequently prescribed medicines worldwide. However, inappropriate utilization of antimicrobials has become one of the principal drivers of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), threatening the effectiveness of modern healthcare. The outpatient setting accounts for a substantial proportion of antimicrobial consumption, making it an important focus for antimicrobial stewardship interventions. Although Sri Lanka has strengthened national policies on antimicrobial stewardship and AMR containment, evidence describing outpatient antimicrobial utilization, particularly in secondary care hospitals, remains limited. Furthermore, few studies have attempted to interpret antimicrobial utilization alongside local communicable disease epidemiology. Objective: To describe the pattern of outpatient antimicrobial utilization at Base Hospital, Maha Oya over a thirteen-month period. Methods: A retrospective descriptive pharmacoepidemiological study was conducted using routinely maintained pharmacy dispensing records of the Outpatient Department (OPD) at Base Hospital Maha Oya, Sri Lanka. Monthly utilization data for all antimicrobial medicines, including antibacterial, antiviral and antifungal agents, dispensed between June 2025 and June 2026 were extracted and analysed. Quarterly communicable disease surveillance reports covering the corresponding period were reviewed to summarize disease trends within the hospital's catchment area. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize antimicrobial utilization, while temporal comparisons between quarterly antimicrobial utilization and communicable disease notifications were performed descriptively. Results: During the study period, 34 antimicrobial preparations comprising antibacterial, antiviral and antifungal agents were dispensed through the outpatient pharmacy. Antibacterial agents constituted the largest proportion of overall antimicrobial utilization, with amoxicillin and co-amoxiclav being the most frequently utilized medicines. Monthly utilization demonstrated noticeable temporal variation throughout the study period. Communicable disease surveillance data identified chickenpox, dengue fever, leptospirosis and tuberculosis as the predominant notifiable diseases reported within the hospital catchment area. Conclusion: This study provides baseline evidence regarding outpatient antimicrobial utilization in a secondary care hospital in Sri Lanka and demonstrates the value of integrating pharmacy utilization data with communicable disease surveillance. The findings highlight opportunities for strengthening antimicrobial stewardship programmes, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and supporting evidence-based prescribing policies within secondary healthcare institutions.

title: eLife Assessment: Tracking West Nile virus dynamics using viral loads from trapped mosquitoes
abstract: Mosquito-borne virus transmission is increasing globally. Due to a lack of effective vaccines or targeted treatments, mitigation relies on reducing human exposure to infectious mosquitoes. Entomological surveillance provides estimates of human risk by quantifying the prevalence of arboviruses in mosquito populations. Testing of pooled mosquitoes with RT-qPCR is often used to infer infection prevalence, however these data are often binarised and ignore semi-quantitative cycle threshold (Ct values) that may provide valuable information on virus kinetics, mosquito infectiousness, and ultimately human risk. West Nile virus (WNV) is a globally distributed arbovirus and endemic to the United States. In this study, we analysed pooled Ct values from retrospective mosquito surveillance and found substantial variation that could not be explained by laboratory factors alone. To understand how underlying viral load and epidemiological dynamics might explain this variation, we developed a multi-scale model linking pooled Ct values to heterogeneous within-host viral kinetics in mosquitoes and birds and seasonal transmission dynamics. Our modelling suggests that Ct values from positive pools might reflect a mixture of potentially infectious and non-infectious mosquitoes, indicating that a substantial proportion of PCR-positive mosquitoes might not contribute to transmission. We then developed a method to estimate mosquito infection prevalence using only pooled Ct values that distinguishes infectious from non-infectious prevalence. Estimates of overall prevalence were comparable to standard methods using binarised data and remained accurate at higher prevalences where standard approaches fail. Overall, these findings demonstrate that entomological viral load data reflect biologically meaningful variation in mosquito infection status that is lost through binarisation. Accounting for heterogeneous mosquito viral kinetics can improve interpretation of surveillance data and estimates of transmission risk, with implications for arbovirus surveillance beyond WNV.

Entomological surveillance provides estimates of human risk by quantifying the prevalence of arboviruses in mosquito populations. Testing of pooled mosquitoes with RT-qPCR is often used to infer infection prevalence, however these data are often binarised and ignore semi-quantitative cycle threshold (Ct values) that may provide valuable information on virus kinetics, mosquito infectiousness, and ultimately human risk. West Nile virus (WNV) is a globally distributed arbovirus and endemic to the United States. In this study, we analysed pooled Ct values from retrospective mosquito surveillance and found substantial variation that could not be explained by laboratory factors alone. To understand how underlying viral load and epidemiological dynamics might explain this variation, we developed a multi-scale model linking pooled Ct values to heterogeneous within-host viral kinetics in mosquitoes and birds and seasonal transmission dynamics. Our modelling suggests that Ct values from positive pools might reflect a mixture of potentially infectious and non-infectious mosquitoes, indicating that a substantial proportion of PCR-positive mosquitoes might not contribute to transmission. We then developed a method to estimate mosquito infection prevalence using only pooled Ct values that distinguishes infectious from non-infectious prevalence. Estimates of overall prevalence were comparable to standard methods using binarised data and remained accurate at higher prevalences where standard approaches fail. Overall, these findings demonstrate that entomological viral load data reflect biologically meaningful variation in mosquito infection status that is lost through binarisation. Accounting for heterogeneous mosquito viral kinetics can improve interpretation of surveillance data and estimates of transmission risk, with implications for arbovirus surveillance beyond WNV.

title: Differentiated LUHMES Cells as a Model to Investigate Neurotropic Arboviruses and Evaluate Host-Directed Therapeutics
abstract: Arthropod-borne viruses such as Alphaviruses and Flaviviruses are the causative agents of severe human disease, highlighted by fatal encephalitis and neurological sequelae in survivors. The lack of FDA-approved vaccines and therapeutics that can prevent or treat these infections results in a significant global disease burden. An important unmet need to address this capability gap is the need for affordable, scalable, clinically relevant human-based neuronal models to study neuroinvasive viruses and evaluate therapeutic options. Here, we described the application of a human neuronal precursor cell model, LUHMES (Lund human mesencephalic) cells, that can be differentiated into dopaminergic midbrain neurons and used to study virus infections. In this study, we demonstrated the susceptibility of LUHMES cells to infection by three arthropod-borne neurotropic viruses: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, dengue virus serotype 2, and West Nile virus. We also demonstrated how the model may be applied to evaluate potential therapeutic options using an FDA-approved small molecule, Omaveloxolone. Finally, we analyzed host cell responses to infection and treatment using gene expression and phospho-signaling analyses. These findings highlight the value of this model to interpret the pathogenic mechanisms of neurotropic viral infections and evaluate potential therapeutic intervention strategies in a clinically relevant in vitro human neuronal model.

title: Clinico-Hematological Evaluation of Bicytopenia in Adults: A Hospital-based Observational Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bicytopenia is defined as a reduction in any two of the three major blood cell lineages and may result from a wide spectrum of infectious, nutritional, hematological, and systemic disorders. Early identification of the underlying etiology is essential for appropriate management. AIMS: To study the etiological spectrum, hematological profile, clinical presentation, and patterns of bicytopenia among patients attending a tertiary care Center. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The study analyzed the clinical and hematological profile of 110 patients with bicytopenia. Patients were categorized based on age, gender, hematological parameters, etiologies, symptoms, and type of bicytopenia. Statistical analysis was performed using the Chi-square test. RESULTS: Patients in the study had a mean age of 41.5 ± 15.42 years with female predominance (54.5%). Viral fever, including dengue, was the leading cause (23.6%), subsequently nutritional deficiency (13.6%) and sepsis (11.8%). Leukopenia with thrombocytopenia was the most common type of bicytopenia (37.3%). Fever was the predominant presenting symptom (48.2%). The type of bicytopenia showed a significant association with of underlying etiology (P < 0.0001). CONCLUSION: Bicytopenia is associated with diverse etiologies ranging from transient infections to serious hematological disorders. Infectious diseases and nutritional deficiencies constituted the major causes in the present study. Recognition of hematological patterns along with systematic clinical evaluation can aid in early diagnosis and timely management.

title: Inflammation and hemostatic system: a selection of involved clinical disorders
abstract: The role of the hemostatic system in host defense underscores the significant connection among coagulation, platelets, and inflammation. Both the hemostatic and the immune systems share a common ancestral origin. During infections, blood coagulation and platelet activation work in tandem with the immune system to combat bacterial and viral threats. Together, they help limit the spread of these pathogens by forming a fibrin clot network that not only kills pathogens but also promotes tissue repair. However, an excessive response is dangerous, as it can lead to both thrombosis and bleeding. The aim of this narrative review is to present the link between inflammation and the hemostatic system across different pathological conditions, such as infectious diseases (sepsis, plague, COVID-19 infection, Ebola, and Dengue virus infection, and malaria) and autoimmune diseases (antiphospholipid syndrome, systemic sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis). Although infectious diseases are characterized by a direct attack on the innate immune system, which in turn activates blood coagulation and platelets, Autoimmune diseases, through antibody production, can induce a coagulative reaction that can generate both thrombosis and fibrosis.

title: Analysis of Prognostic Indicators in Fever Associated with Thrombocytopenia Among Children Up to 12 Years
abstract: Fever associated with thrombocytopenia is a common clinical presentation in paediatric practice, particularly in regions with a high prevalence of infectious diseases. This study aimed to analyse prognostic indicators and clinical outcomes in children up to 12 years presenting with fever and thrombocytopenia. A cross-sectional observational study was conducted on 150 children admitted with fever (>99.9°F) and platelet counts below 150,000/μL at Pushpagiri Medical College and Hospital Research Institute, Kerala. Detailed clinical evaluation, laboratory investigations, and outcome assessment were performed. Dengue fever emerged as the most prevalent etiology (41.3%), followed by non-dengue viral fever (25.3%), enteric fever (14%), sepsis (11.4%), and malaria (8%). Most children exhibited mild to moderate thrombocytopenia (74%). The majority (74.7%) improved with supportive management, while 18.7% required ICU admission. Complications such as bleeding or shock occurred in 5.3% of cases, and the mortality rate was 1.3%. Younger age groups and severe thrombocytopenia were more frequently associated with adverse outcomes. The findings underscore the need for early identification of high-risk children, careful monitoring, and timely intervention to prevent complications. Strengthening diagnostic practices and clinician awareness can significantly improve outcomes in paediatric febrile thrombocytopenia. Keywords: Fever; Thrombocytopenia; Children; Prognostic indicators; Dengue fever; Paediatric infections; Platelet count; Clinical outcomes; Complications; ICU admission.

title: Etiological Spectrum of Acute Febrile Illness in a Tertiary Care Hospital in Assam, India: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Introduction: Acute Febrile Illness (AFI) encompasses a spectrum of conditions marked by fever, often caused by various infectious agents. The aetiological diversity poses challenges in diagnosis and treatment, particularly in regions with limited diagnostic resources. Aim: To evaluate the spectrum of pathogens causing AFI with or without rash in patients. Materials and Methods: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted from January 2024 to December 2024 on 1,544 patients who had attended Lakhimpur Medical College and Hospital, North Lakhimpur, Assam, India. Patients with fever (≥ 37.5°C) with or without rash were enrolled. Serological investigations for Measles, Rubella, Dengue, Varicella-zoster, Chikungunya viruses, Japanese Encephalitis (JE), Orientia tsutsugamushi, Leptospira, and Hepatitis viruses were performed using Enzyme-linked Immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and Rapid Detection Testing (RDT) kits. Data analysis was performed using both descriptive and inferential methods. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant. Results: Fever was prevalent in all 1,544 (100%) cases, followed by 856 (55.44%) cases of headache, 636 (41.19%) with cough, 476 (30.83%) with vomiting, 347 (22.47%) with abdominal pain, 59 (3.82%) cases with dysentery, 52 (3.37%) with diarrhoea, 46 (2.98%) cases with unconsciousness, and 21 (1.36%) cases presented with rash. Fever was observed in combination with headache in 856 (55.44%), with cough in 636 (41.19%), with bodyache in 481 (31.15%), and with vomiting in 476 (30.83%) cases. The study identified seasonal variations in infection rates, with peaks during the monsoon months. The majority of positive cases were attributed to Scrub Typhus 133/817 (16.28%), followed by Leptospirosis 129/473 (27.27%), Dengue 84/1273 (6.59%), and JE 20/87 (22.99%), while some had co-infection. Conclusion: The study underscores the importance of integrated clinical and laboratory approaches in diagnosing AFI. Scrub typhus, leptospirosis, and dengue were identified as major causes, emphasising the need for enhanced surveillance and diagnostic capabilities.
journal: Journal of Clinical and Diagnostic Research

title: Research Advances and Future Perspectives of Point-of-Care Detection Technologies and Biosensors for Mosquito-Borne Viruses
abstract: Mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses, place a substantial burden on diagnostic services, especially where molecular laboratories are inaccessible or slow to return results. Point-of-care biosensors could reduce turnaround times and bring testing closer to patients in primary care, outbreak response, and field settings. This review critically examines nucleic acid amplification, CRISPR-assisted assays, lateral-flow platforms, microfluidic systems, electrochemical and optical biosensors, paper-based devices, and smartphone-enabled readouts. These technologies are evaluated in terms of sample preparation, analytical sensitivity and specificity, matrix interference, multiplexing, workflow integration, cost, and clinical validation. Overall, nucleic-acid-amplification and CRISPR-assisted platforms often achieve low reported detection limits under controlled conditions; lateral-flow and paper-based devices offer relatively simple and minimally instrumented workflows; and microfluidic, electrochemical, and smartphone-enabled systems support increasing levels of workflow integration, quantitative readout, and connectivity. However, few platforms currently integrate these advantages into a fully integrated and clinically validated “sample-to-result” workflow. Due to sample heterogeneity, viral strains, reference methods, assay conditions, and disparities in reporting practices, conducting meaningful cross-study comparisons remains challenging. Limited comparisons and insufficient prospective clinical and field validation further restrict the assessment of practical diagnostic utility. Therefore, strong analytical performance alone should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical validity. Priority directions include unified definitions of performance and reporting units, standardized validation protocols and external quality assessment, prospective multi-site evaluation using representative populations and specimens, and earlier consideration of manufacturing scalability, reagent stability, quality systems, and applicable regulatory requirements. Future platforms should integrate simplified sample preparation, multiplex detection, objective digital or AI-assisted interpretation, and secure connectivity while demonstrating measurable benefits for patient management and outbreak surveillance.

Uji T-test dan uji populasi besar chi-square menunjukkan bahwa usia (χ2 = 6.341, df = 3 p = 0,093) dan jenis kelamin (χ2 = 1.675; df = 2 p = 0,432) tidak menunjukkan asosiasi yang signifikan secara statistik. Mengidentifikasi adanya hubungan antara determinan sosial (pendidikan dan pekerjaan) dan pengetahuan pencegahan DBD yang secara statistik signifikan, sedangkan usia dan jenis kelamin tidak menunjukkan signifikansi statistik. Hasil ini menunjukkan bahwa intervensi yang menargetkan pengetahuan perlu mempertimbangkan stratifikasi pendidikan dan akses informasi berbasis pekerjaan. Namun, hanya pengetahuan yang baik tidak cukup karena pendekatan baru harus diperoleh melalui pengetahuan agar tujuan mulia untuk melanjutkan sikap dan perilaku pencegahan dapat tercapai. title: Penerapan Manajemen Cairan pada Pasien DHF dengan Risiko Hipovolemia di RS X Tangerang Selatan
abstract: Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever merupakan infeksi virus dengue yang dapat meningkatkan permeabilitas kapiler, menyebabkan kebocoran plasma, penurunan volume intravaskular, dan risiko hipovolemia. Studi kasus ini bertujuan menggambarkan penerapan manajemen cairan pada pasien dengan Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever yang mengalami risiko hipovolemia melalui perbandingan kondisi klinis dua pasien. Desain yang digunakan adalah studi kasus deskriptif dengan pendekatan proses keperawatan pada dua pasien di ruang rawat inap RS X Tangerang Selatan pada Juni 2026. Data diperoleh melalui wawancara, observasi, pemeriksaan fisik, dokumentasi rekam medis, pemeriksaan laboratorium, serta pemantauan asupan dan keluaran cairan. Intervensi mengacu pada Standar Intervensi Keperawatan Indonesia dan dilaksanakan selama tiga kali dua puluh empat jam. Hasil menunjukkan bahwa pasien pertama mengalami tekanan darah 90/70 mmHg, nadi 102 kali/menit, mukosa kering, turgor menurun, dan hematokrit 40,8%, sehingga pemantauan difokuskan pada stabilitas hemodinamik dan volume intravaskular. Pasien kedua memiliki hemodinamik relatif stabil, tetapi mengalami stomatitis yang menghambat asupan oral, hematokrit 44,4%, serta trombositopenia berat hingga 25.000/mm3 disertai petekie. Setelah intervensi, kondisi klinis dan status hidrasi kedua pasien membaik, dengan keseimbangan cairan positif sebesar +937,5 mL dan +1.105 mL. Kadar trombosit saat pemulangan meningkat menjadi 57.000/mm3 dan 41.000/mm3. Manajemen cairan yang disertai pemantauan hemodinamik, hidrasi, keseimbangan cairan, dan laboratorium membantu mempertahankan volume sirkulasi serta mencegah perburukan hipovolemia. Pendekatan perlu disesuaikan dengan karakteristik klinis setiap pasien.

title: Intuitionistic Fuzzy Soft Set Framework for Diagnosing Infectious Diseases
abstract: The difficulty of overlapping symptoms in medical diagnosis makes it challenging to precisely identify the diseases, which can lead to delayed or improper treatment. For example, malaria, dengue, and typhoid fever share common symptoms such as headache, high fever, nausea, muscle pain, pain in joints, and fatigue. Growing population, poor hygiene, increase in urbanization, and climate change lead to the intensified spread of typhoid, dengue, and malaria. Fuzzy theory deals with the uncertainty and imprecision in processing the data and decision-making. Various models utilize fuzzy sets to deal with several difficult components of medical diagnosis. Fuzzy soft sets are an extension of traditional fuzzy sets intended to deal with the alternative's parameterized values in the process of decision-making. Fuzzy intuitionistic sets enhance the concept of fuzzy sets by including the degrees of membership, non-membership, and hesitation, which provide a more sophisticated way of simulating ambiguous information. When uncertain data becomes more complex, the notion of intuitionistic fuzzy soft sets arises as a combination of intuitionistic fuzzy sets and fuzzy soft sets. In this chapter, we analyze the concepts of fuzzy soft sets, intuitionistic fuzzy sets, and intuitionistic fuzzy soft sets. We begin by discussing the basic definitions and operations related to these sets, and distinguish them from ordinary fuzzy sets and soft sets. Moreover, this will be followed by the demonstration through some interesting examples, for each of these sets. This will showcase the significance of these sets in managing uncertainty and ambiguity, in practical situations. Finally, we present an application of an intuitionistic fuzzy soft set in the diagnosis of infectious diseases such as malaria, dengue, and typhoid fever.

title: Karakter Tempat Perindukan dan Status Resistensi Nyamuk Aedes aegypti (Linnaeus, 1762) di Kelurahan Sorosutan Terhadap Permethrin Secara CDC Bottle Bioassay
abstract: Kota Yogyakarta merupakan wilayah endemik Demam Berdarah Dengue (DBD) sebagai salah satu penyakit tular vektor. Berbagai strategi pengendalian vektor telah dilakukan untuk penyakit ini, diantaranya dengan penggunaan insektisida sintetis. Namun, penggunaan insektisida dalam jangka waktu yang lama dan terus menerus, serta penggunaan dosis yang tidak terkendali dapat menyebabkan resistensi pada populasi nyamuk. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mempelajari karakter tempat perindukan dan status resistensi nyamuk Ae. aegypti dari Kelurahan Sorosutan terhadap permethrin secara CDC Bottle Bioassay. Observasi karakteristik perindukan dan koleksi telur nyamuk dilakukan pada 100 rumah warga secara random. Rearing nyamuk dan uji resistensi dilakukan di Laboratorium Entomologi dan Pengendalian Vektor, Balai Besar Laboratorium Kesehatan Masyarakat, Yogyakarta. Karakter perindukan yang ditemukan adalah berupa badan air terbuka dan larva paling banyak ditemukan di vas tanaman, bak mandi semen, ember penampung air hujan, dan barang bekas (kemasan plastik, toples). Di Kelurahan Sorosutan, Indeks Entomologi menunjukkan nilai CI sebesar 23,33%, HI 37%, dan BI 42%, yang mengindikasikan bahwa wilayah ini termasuk dengan kepadatan vektor tinggi. Hasil uji resistensi menunjukkan bahwa nyamuk Ae. aegypti telah resisten terhadap permethrin pada dosis 1x (0,75μg/botol) dan 5x (3,75μg/botol), kondisi ini berpotensi sedang sampai tinggi terjadinya transmisi penyakit.

title: From Structure to Therapy: A Comprehensive Review on the Pharmacological Applications of Tertiary Amides
abstract: Tertiary amides have attracted increasing interest from pharmaceutical researchers because of their particular structural characteristics, high chemical stability, and wide variety of biological activities. Tertiary amides are present in many bioactive molecules and represent an important motif for new drug development. This review systematically discusses recent advances in the therapeutic uses of tertiary amide derivatives. Recent studies indicate that tertiary amides have great potential as anticancer agents with proven activity against gastric cancer, via the modulation of NEDDylation pathways and inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinases, leading to disruption of cancer cell proliferation and survival. Furthermore, current research shows that tertiary amide derivatives are potent against several viruses, such as the hepatitis C virus, bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV), dengue virus, and Tacaribe virus. These findings indicate that tertiary amide derivatives serve as effective and versatile antiviral agents for preventing and treating numerous emerging and persistent viral infections. Additionally, many tertiary amides exhibit strong activity against various pathogenic bacteria, underscoring their importance in the global effort to combat antimicrobial resistance. Several physicochemical factors that determine tertiary amides in drug discovery programs include lipophilicity, conformational rigidity, and metabolic stability; all these physicochemical parameters improve bioavailability and 'drug-like' characteristics, making these compounds ideal candidates for optimization in drug discovery programs. Overall, current evidence demonstrates the broad applicability of tertiary amides and their potential for new drug development. This review provides insights into the design and development of therapeutic agents based on tertiary amide scaffolds.

title: Mathematical Modeling of Japanese Encephalitis: Multi-Host Transmission Dynamics and Intervention Strategies
abstract: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) transmission involves complex interactions among Culex mosquitoes, amplifying pig hosts, reservoir wading birds, humans, and environmental conditions, complicating quantitative assessment of transmission dynamics and intervention effectiveness. We developed a deterministic, fourteen-compartment One Health mathematical framework that integrates these interconnected host vector populations and their epidemiological states. The model incorporates temperature-dependent mosquito biting, seasonal transmission, human vaccination, pig biosecurity, environmental barriers, and mosquito-control interventions. Mathematical properties were established through analyses of non-negativity, boundedness, biologically feasible equilibria, local and global stability, and optimal control. District-specific simulations were conducted for Bellary, Udupi, Kolkata, and Purba Bardhaman during the August transmission period. Intervention scenarios were evaluated, and global sensitivity analysis was performed using 500 Latin hypercube samples with partial rank correlation coefficients. Model outputs were also compared with district-level surveillance observations. Vaccination-adjusted basic reproduction numbers were 0.905 in Bellary, 0.965 in Udupi, 1.817 in Kolkata, and 0.885 in Purba Bardhaman, with only Kolkata exceeding the epidemic threshold. Under maximum intervention, total infections decreased by 80.6%, 96.8%, 80.5%, and 72.2%, respectively, while infected mosquito populations declined to zero across all four settings. In Kolkata, vaccinating 3.6 million individuals with dose series II reduced the reproduction number from 1.817 to 0.9846, whereas population-wide dose series I vaccination alone was insufficient to reduce it below unity. Sensitivity analysis identified mosquito recruitment, temperature-dependent biting, carrying capacity, mosquito mortality, density-dependent regulation, and mosquito-to-human transmission as major determinants of peak human infection. Overall, the framework demonstrates heterogeneity in JEV transmission and intervention effectiveness and provides a mathematically grounded One Health approach for comparative evaluation of integrated control strategies.

title: Local Linear Estimation for Covariate-Dependent Coefficients Model in Disease Mapping.
abstract: Spatial regression effects may depend on covariates in disease-mapping models. For example, the association between infectious disease incidence and risk factors may vary according to climatic factors, such as time, season, and temperature. In this study, we aim to develop a spatial model that accounts simultaneously for the spatial and varying effects of covariates believed to modulate the spatial association. We employ a local linear estimation method to estimate covariate-dependent coefficients in a model for excess zero counts. The local linear estimator effectively smooths covariate-dependent coefficient estimation. Comprehensive simulation studies were conducted to evaluate the performance of the local linear estimators, and reported dengue cases in villages in Kaohsiung City from January 2014 to December 2015 are used to inform our proposed method for practical use in real-world applications.

title: Diagnostic Challenges of West Nile Virus Serology in Japanese Encephalitis-Endemic Regions
abstract: Background: In South Korea, where Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is endemic, autochthonous human West Nile virus (WNV) infections have not been confirmed.Interpreting WNV serological results is difficult owing to cross-reactive antibodies.This study examined the relationship between WNV enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) reactivity and neutralization in paired serum samples from patients with confirmed JEV.Methods: Thirty-one pairs of acute and convalescent serum samples from laboratoryconfirmed JEV patients from 2021 to 2023 were analyzed.JEV-and WNV-specific IgM and IgG responses were measured by ELISA.Changes in immune status ratio (ISR) values and inter-virus correlations were assessed.Neutralization activity was evaluated using plaque reduction neutralization test (PRNT) to compare temporal changes and titers of JEV and WNV.Concordance between WNV ELISA and PRNT results was analyzed by cross-tabulation, regression, and nonparametric tests.Results: ELISA indices showed significantly higher ISR values in the convalescent sera compared with those in the acute sera.JEV and WNV ISR values positively correlated within the same antibody class.In contrast, PRNT analysis showed that JEV neutralizing titers increased during convalescence across all tested JEV genotypes, whereas WNV log 2 (PRNT 50 ) values remained generally low and increased only modestly from the acute to the convalescent phase.Across all genotypes, JEV log 2 (PRNT 50 ) values consistently exceeded WNV values, with regression slopes < 1, indicating a persistent functional gap between the two viruses.Cross-tabulation of WNV ELISA and PRNT results showed substantial discordance: a subset of ELISA-positive sera lacked detectable WNV neutralization, whereas some ELISA-negative sera showed measurable neutralizing activity.Conclusion: JEV infection induced cross-reactive WNV ELISA responses, raising median WNV ISR from 4.5 to 14.1 for IgM and from 1.2 to 3.3 for IgG.WNV neutralizing activity remained relatively low, with median WNV log 2 (PRNT 50 ) values increasing only from 0.0 to 6.3.The discrepancy between ELISA and PRNT results suggests that WNV ELISA detects cross-binding antibodies but does not reliably indicate neutralization, highlighting the need for confirmatory tests, such as PRNT, in JEV-endemic areas.

title: Zika Endemicity Lowers the HIV Invasion Threshold: A Mathematical Model of Zika‐HIV Coinfection
abstract: ABSTRACT The coexistence of Zika virus (ZIKV) and HIV across tropical areas presents important research opportunities to examine how vector‐borne pathogens affect trends of sexually transmitted diseases. We create a detailed mathematical model that combines vector‐borne transmission with sexual transmission, antiretroviral treatment, coinfection disease development, human movement across multiple population systems, and seasonal changes in mosquito populations, which are forced by climate. The research presents a new concept that defines an effective coinfection invasion reproduction number that describes how HIV establishes itself in populations where the Zika virus circulates. Analytical results demonstrate that endemic Zika transmission decreases the HIV invasion threshold, which allows HIV to survive even when the classical HIV reproduction number falls below one. The analysis of the center manifold and bifurcation demonstrates that the threshold reduction happens through forward transcritical bifurcations. The coinfection persistence patterns reveal three main factors: mosquito biting intensity, HIV transmission rate, and ART‐related parameters, while spatial connectivity and climate variability increase the epidemic burden. The study shows that co‐endemic areas need climate‐aware treatments based on human mobility patterns to create successful intervention strategies.

title: Multiple orthoflaviviruses secrete sfRNA in mosquito saliva to promote transmission by inhibiting MDA5-mediated early interferon response
abstract: Abstract Numerous orthoflaviviruses transmitted through the bites of different mosquito species infect more than 500 million people annually. Skin infection at the bite site represents a critical and conserved step in transmission and a deeper understanding of this process will promote the design of broad-spectrum interventions. Here, we identify and characterize a transmission-enhancing viral factor in mosquito saliva that is shared across orthoflaviviruses. Saliva from West Nile virus-infected Culex and Zika virus-infected Aedes contains a viral non-coding RNA, subgenomic flaviviral RNA (sfRNA), within lipid vesicles distinct from virions. Higher concentration of sfRNA in infectious saliva positively correlates with infection intensity in human cells and skin explants. Early sfRNA delivery into transmission-relevant skin cell types and human skin explant demonstrate that sfRNA is responsible for the infection enhancement. Co-inoculation of sfRNA in a mouse model of transmission enhanced skin infection and worsened disease severity, supporting the role of salivary sfRNA as a transmission-enhancer. Mechanistically, salivary sfRNA attenuates early interferon response in human skin cells and skin explants by disrupting MDA5 signaling. Our results, derived from two distinct orthoflaviviruses and supported by prior studies, establish salivary sfRNA as a pan-orthoflavivirus transmission-enhancing factor driven by a conserved viral non-coding RNA.

full_text: Abstract Background Dengue fever (DF) is a viral infection spread by mosquitoes and is one of the most frequently reported infectious diseases in Saudi Arabia, particularly in Jeddah. Despite recurring outbreaks, recent data on the clinical characteristics, seasonal variation, and outcomes of affected patients in the region remain limited. This study aimed to assess the clinical symptoms, laboratory findings, and outcomes of patients diagnosed with dengue fever who presented to the emergency department of King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC) in Jeddah, a tertiary care center. Methods A retrospective review was conducted on all medical records of all patients aged ≥ 14 years with serologically confirmed dengue fever who presented to the emergency department of King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC), Jeddah, between August 2022 and August 2024. Demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and patient outcomes were extracted from electronic records and analysed using descriptive statistics with exploratory inferential analyses where appropriate, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results The study included 319 patients (mean age 45.7 ± 18.4 years; 53.3% male). The most common presenting symptoms were fever (95.3%), vomiting (44.5%), headache (44.5%), and nausea (43.3%). Thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 150 × 109/L) was observed in 56.4% of patients at presentation, and elevated alanine transaminase levels were identified in 69.1%. The most common comorbidities were hypertension (25.1%) and diabetes (23.5%). Nearly half of the patients (46.7%) required hospitalization, with a mean length of stay of 3.8 days, and no mortality was reported. Most cases occurred in spring (44%) and winter (32%), reflecting a distinct seasonal pattern. Conclusion Dengue fever in Jeddah primarily affects middle-aged adults and commonly presents with fever and gastrointestinal symptoms. The observed seasonal clustering during winter and spring suggests a potential influence of climatic factors on transmission, while the high prevalence of diabetes and hypertension underscores the importance of managing comorbidities in affected patients. These findings support the development of integrated clinical and environmental strategies to enhance dengue control in western Saudi Arabia. Despite recurring outbreaks, recent data on the clinical characteristics, seasonal variation, and outcomes of affected patients in the region remain limited. This study aimed to assess the clinical symptoms, laboratory findings, and outcomes of patients diagnosed with dengue fever who presented to the emergency department of King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC) in Jeddah, a tertiary care center. Methods A retrospective review was conducted on all medical records of all patients aged ≥ 14 years with serologically confirmed dengue fever who presented to the emergency department of King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC), Jeddah, between August 2022 and August 2024. Demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and patient outcomes were extracted from electronic records and analysed using descriptive statistics with exploratory inferential analyses where appropriate, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results The study included 319 patients (mean age 45.7 ± 18.4 years; 53.3% male). The most common presenting symptoms were fever (95.3%), vomiting (44.5%), headache (44.5%), and nausea (43.3%). Thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 150 × 109/L) was observed in 56.4% of patients at presentation, and elevated alanine transaminase levels were identified in 69.1%. The most common comorbidities were hypertension (25.1%) and diabetes (23.5%). Nearly half of the patients (46.7%) required hospitalization, with a mean length of stay of 3.8 days, and no mortality was reported. Most cases occurred in spring (44%) and winter (32%), reflecting a distinct seasonal pattern. Conclusion Dengue fever in Jeddah primarily affects middle-aged adults and commonly presents with fever and gastrointestinal symptoms. The observed seasonal clustering during winter and spring suggests a potential influence of climatic factors on transmission, while the high prevalence of diabetes and hypertension underscores the importance of managing comorbidities in affected patients. These findings support the development of integrated clinical and environmental strategies to enhance dengue control in western Saudi Arabia. This study found a low seroprevalence of dengue virus (6.4%) among febrile patients in Nigeria's Federal Capital Territory, alongside a high prevalence of malaria (66%), highlighting the need for targeted public health interventions to improve disease surveillance and vector control. Abstract Background Dengue fever (DF) is a mosquito-borne viral infection that poses a significant and growing public health concern in Nigeria. Despite its increasing incidence, the burden and interaction of dengue with other febrile illnesses, such as malaria, remain poorly characterised. Objective and method This study aimed to determine the seroprevalence rates of DENV infection, assess its co-morbidity with malaria, and identify associated socio-demographic and environmental risk factors in a cross-section of 250 febrile patients attending primary healthcare facilities in two local area councils of the Federal Capital Territory, Nigeria. Samples were screened for Malaria (using RDT) and DF antibodies (IgG and IgM) and antigen (NS1). Result This study revealed a relatively low prevalence of DF among febrile patients. The IgG seropositivity rate was 5.2% (n = 13/250), IgM antibodies was detected in one patient (0.4%), and the NS1 antigen was detected in two patients (0.8%), indicating ongoing infection. Two-thirds of participants (66%, n = 165/250) tested positive for malaria. Co-infection of DF and malaria was detected in only one patient. The majority of the participants lived in close proximity to refuse dumps (57.6%, n = 144/250), 67.6% (n = 169/250) routinely cleared household refuse within 48 h, and 50% (n = 125/250) slept under insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs). Participants who frequently sleep under ITNs had lower (OR: 0.28; 95% CI 0.07, 1.06; p = 0.041) dengue seropositivity compared to those who do not sleep under ITNs. Although statistically insignificant, our regression analysis also revealed that participants residing within the Abuja municipal area council were more likely (OR: 7.75; 95% CI 0.99, 60.59; p = 0.011) to test positive for DF IgG than in Bwari. Conclusion This study revealed a relatively low prevalence of DF, a high prevalence of malaria in febrile patients, and co-morbidity of malaria and DF in one patient, which complicates the diagnosis and treatment of DF. These patients lived in environmental conditions that promote mosquito breeding. The findings underscore the need for prompt and targeted interventions, including community education on DF, improved distribution and use of ITNs, and the adoption of vector control measures. 1 Background Dengue fever (DF) is a viral haemorrhagic disease and a significant public health concern in Nigeria. It is the most rapidly spreading arboviral infection worldwide [1]. This arthropod-borne illness is caused by Dengue virus (DENV), a member of the family Flaviviridae. DENV is a primary human pathogen transmitted by the mosquito vectors Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus [2, 3]. It is a small, non-segmented, single-stranded, positive-sense, enveloped RNA virus measuring 50 nm in diameter [4]. DENV exists in four serotypes (DENV1 to DENV4) [4, 5]. There is no cross-immunity between the four serotypes; infection with one serotype does not guarantee immunity against the other serotypes. Individuals may be infected four times, each time with a different serotype [5,6,7,8,9]. About 2.5 billion people are estimated to be living in DENV endemic areas worldwide [10], with DENV infecting an estimated 100–400 million humans each year [10]. Between January 2024 and April 2025, there were approximately 17 million cases of DF, which resulted in approximately 60,000 severe cases and 12,375 deaths [11]. The clinical presentation of DF often overlaps with malaria, making it challenging to distinguish between the two diseases, especially in malaria-endemic regions. The disease mostly presents as an acute flu-like illness, which often develops into fatal complications, called severe dengue (dengue haemorrhagic fever or dengue with shock syndrome) [10, 11]. The other form of the disease presents as uncomplicated (classical DF), which appears in two phases of illness, starting suddenly 3–8 days after the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito and characterised by prodromal malaria-like symptoms (fever, headache, severe malaise, lumbosacral aching, and generalised muscle, joint, or bone pain) [2, 10]. These clinical malaria fever presentations in malaria-endemic regions contributed to over 70% of the febrile illnesses being treated as presumptive malaria [10, 11]. Globally, the risk of dengue is similar across regions, countries, and within countries [12]. Factors associated with an increasing global burden include changing distribution and increasing abundance of the mosquito vectors; climate change, and periodic weather phenomena leading to heavy precipitation, humidity, and rising temperatures, favouring vector reproduction and virus transmission. In addition, the burden of DF could be influenced by changes in the circulating serotypes within a country, fragile health systems amid political and financial instability in countries facing complex humanitarian crises, and large-scale population movements that carry the mosquito vectors, impairing the public health response [12]. Nigeria’s poor surveillance and underreporting of DF (and other diseases) continues to be hampered due to multiple, concurrent outbreaks, limited resources (including shortages of good-quality dengue diagnostic kits for early disease detection), a lack of trained clinical and vector control staff, and poor community awareness of the disease [10, 12]. In addition, diagnosis of dengue may be complicated by a clinical presentation very similar to malaria and other flaviviruses, such as Zika and chikungunya. While the former is endemic in Nigeria, chikungunya is not, but has been reported in Nigeria [13, 14]. The true burden of DF in Nigeria remains uncertain, although a systematic review of 25 studies on DENV IgM and IgG reported a pooled prevalence of 16.8% and 34.7%, respectively [15]. A previous study conducted within Nigeria’s Federal Capital Territory (FCT) found an IgG seropositivity prevalence of 43.3% among 171 patients presenting with febrile illnesses at a tertiary health facility [16]. As there is currently no licensed vaccine for DF in Nigeria, public health efforts primarily focus on Mosquito vector control [16]. Clinically, early detection of DF remains challenging due to the limited availability of diagnostic tools, its clinical similarity to other febrile illnesses (particularly malaria), non-inclusion in routine practices in the clinics, and low awareness among healthcare personnel [17]. In addition, Nigeria is particularly vulnerable to DF and other mosquito-borne diseases due to rapid urbanisation, poor waste management, and environmental conditions that support mosquito breeding. Given these challenges, the study aims to assess the prevalence of dengue in febrile patients and identify key risk factors in Nigeria’s Federal Capital Territory. 2 Methods 2.1 Ethical considerations Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the Health Research Ethics Committee of the Federal Capital Territory Administration (Approval number FHREC/2022/01/224/14-11-22). Informed consent was obtained from each participant after the attending healthcare worker provided a brief description of the study. The attending healthcare workers in the selected facilities were initially trained. All participants were informed that they would participate in the study without prejudice, their personal identifying information was anonymised, and participation in the study had no impact on the quality of the healthcare service they would receive. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki [18]. Informed consent for children under the age of 16 was obtained from the parent or legal guardian, and none of their personal identifying information was obtained. The study abided by all the ethical protocols in children under 5, including a smaller sample volume and using a smaller gauge needle. 2.2 Study area The study was conducted in the surburbs of the FCT, Nigeria among patients attending 16 Primary Health Centres primary healthcare facilities in two of the six Local Government Areas (LGA) of the FCT: Abuja Municipal Area Council (AMAC, n = 156) and Bwari (n = 94) (Fig. 1). The two LGAs were selected due to their varying levels of sanitation and mosquito control measures, providing a diverse set of environmental and socio-demographic conditions. They have a population of 2.3 million inhabitants and an area of 7315 km2. The FCT is located north of the river Niger and East of the river Benue and lies between latitudes 8.25 and 9.20 north of the equator and longitude 6.45 and 7.39 east of GMT. Within AMAC, nine health facilities were selected [Apo Primary Health Care (PHC)—15; Gidan Mangoro PHC—28; Lugbe PHC—18; Jikwoyi Medical Centre—13; Kabusa PHC—9; Karu PHC—28; Kuchingoro PHC—32; Piwoyi PHC—10; Pyakassa PHC—9] and seven facilities were selected from Bwari LGA (Byazhin PHC—26; Deedee PHC—8; Dawaki PHC—8; Dutshe Alhaji PHC—10; Dutshe Makaranta PHC—9; Mpape PHC—40; Old Deedee PHC—11). 2.3 Study population and design This study was conducted as a healthcare facility-based and cross-sectional survey of febrile patients presenting at these primary health centres between November 2022 and May 2023. The study population consisted of 250 consenting patients with symptoms of febrile illnesses with body temperature ≥ 38 °C among 16 primary healthcare facilities in FCT, Abuja. The inclusion criteria included all consenting individuals of both sexes, aged ≥ 2 years, who were residents within communities serviced by the selected primary healthcare facilities. Exclusion criteria included nonconsenting individuals, those with a prior diagnosis of DF, individuals with immunodeficiency disorders or use of immunosuppressive medication, pregnant women, chronic illnesses or conditions that may affect antibodies, and infants aged < 2 years. A sample size of 250 blood samples was arrived at based on a previously estimated prevalence rate of 43% [16], a 94% confidence interval (CI), and a 6% margin of error. The decision to adopt a 94% CI was guided by the pragmatic constraints of our study setting, including limited resources, time-bound data collection, and restricted facility access. A 94% CI marginally reduces the required sample size while retaining a statistically robust precision level, with only a negligible increase in tolerated uncertainty (1%). 2.4 Data collection Data were collected using an interviewer-administered structured questionnaire. Trained interviewers who were mostly domiciled community healthcare extension workers in these healthcare facilities were trained and collected data from participating patients. The survey instrument was developed for this study and initially pre-validated by two independent academic reviewers, and was later pre-tested before the commencement of sampling and data collection. The survey instrument obtained information on socio-demographic information (including age, gender, and level of education) and information on risk practices that could be associated with mosquito-borne diseases. The survey instrument can be accessed in the supplementary file. 2.5 Dengue fever screening assays Five millilitres (5 ml) of venous blood was collected aseptically from each study participant. No personally identifiable data was collected. Properly packaged samples were transported immediately to the national reference laboratory after collection, followed by separation by centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 5 min. The resulting sera were dispensed into 500 μL cryovial tubes. The serum samples were screened using the Dengue IgG/IgM rapid test kit (Biopanda Reagent Ltd, Belfast, Northern Ireland) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The results were recorded as either positive or negative for Dengue IgG or IgM, or both. Further analysis of the samples was done using antigen detection using the immuno-chromatographic technique, which detects the presence of the non-structural glycoprotein (NS1) as described previously [16]. Prior to testing, the Biopanda Dengue NS1 Rapid Test kits were validated with stored NS1-positive dengue sera of the National Reference Laboratory, Abuja. Sealed immuno-chromatographic kits were opened, and 75μL of the test serum sample was added to the specimen area according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Results were read after a 10-minute incubation period as positive or negative. While these diagnostic assays are effective, their cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses like Zika and chikungunya must be considered when interpreting results. 2.6 Case definition and diagnostic markers According to the World Health Organization, a suspected case of DF is defined as a person living in or travelling to a dengue-endemic area presenting with acute fever (2–7 days) and at least two of the following: Nausea or vomiting, rash, aches and pain (headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia), Leukopenia (White Blood Count < 5000/mm), positive torniquet test or petechiae, or other signs (e.g. abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding). Based on the three diagnostic markers (NS1, IgM, and IgG), cases can be classified as: confirmed (a suspected case with laboratory confirmation of positive NS1) – typified as an active infection, or probable cases typified as recent infection (IgM positive) or past infection (IgG positive). 2.7 Malaria records The results of the malaria parasite (MP) test conducted at the health facility for the sampled patients were obtained after the test was used for the empirical treatment of the patients. Only the test results (positive or negative) were extracted, and no personal identifying information was obtained. 2.8 Data analysis Test results and survey data were analysed and interpreted using SPSS software (version 29). We conducted descriptive statistics and presented the qualitative data as frequencies and percentages, and the quantitative data as mean ± standard deviation. Additionally, Chi-square tests were used to assess associations between categorical variables, and we performed bivariable logistic regression analysis to test for the association between each of the socio-demographic variables and Dengue seropositivity to IgG. The inferences made from this study were based on the output of the bivariable regression analysis at p < 0.05. The map was generated using QGIS v. 3.38. 3 Result 3.1 Study participants The presence of dengue IgM and IgG antibodies was evaluated in 250 serum samples. A larger proportion of samples was collected from healthcare facilities in the AMAC (62.4%, n = 156/250). Approximately two-thirds (68%, n = 170/250) of the samples were obtained from female patients. One-third (34.8%, n = 87/250) were obtained from febrile patients aged between 19 and 29 years. Descriptive analysis of sociodemographic variables revealed that the patients had different educational levels, marital statuses, and occupations (Table 1). 3.2 Prevalence of malaria and dengue fever antibodies Of the 250 febrile patients, 20% (n = 50) presented to a primary healthcare centre with fever that started a week prior to presentation. Most of the other patients had fever for a longer duration and were likely to have self-medicated before presenting to a healthcare centre. The overall seroprevalence of DF markers in the samples was 6.4% (n = 16/250). The IgG seropositivity rate was 5.2% (n = 13/250). Only 1 patient had a recent (or ongoing) dengue infection as evidenced by the presence of IgM (0.4%, n = 1/250). The NS1 antigen was detected in two patients (0.8%, n = 2/250), with both patients negative for IgM and IgG. No patient tested positive for both IgM and IgG or combinations of the NS1 antigen, IgG, and IgM antibodies. Approximately two-thirds (66%, n = 165/250) of febrile patients tested positive for malaria RDT (Table 2). A single patient had co-infection and tested positive for both malaria and recent DF (IgM). There was no association between the occurrence of malaria and DF IgG (p = 0.403) (Table 4). 3.3 Risk factors for dengue fever transmission Analysis of risk practices revealed that more than half (57.6%, n = 144) of the 250 febrile patients had refuse bins (dumps) around their households. Two-thirds (67.6%, n = 169/250) routinely cleared refuse within their immediate household within 48 h. Half of patients (50%, n = 125/250) slept under insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs). A quarter of patients (26%, n = 60/250) were able to properly store water before domestic usage. As the study was conducted in the suburbs of the FCT, 54% (n = 135/250) and 32.4% (n = 81/250) of patients had open drainages with stagnant water and bushy weeds around their household, respectively (Table 3). Of the 10 variables tested, only two variables were significantly associated with the likelihood of higher seropositivity to DF. The bivariable regression analysis revealed that patients living within the AMAC were 7.75 times (95% CI 0.99, 60.59; p = 0.011) more likely to test positive for DF IgG than those in the Bwari local council. Our analysis also revealed that the use of ITNs was significantly associated with lower DF seropositivity, as patients who routinely slept under ITNs were less likely (OR: 0.28; 95% CI 0.07, 1.06; p = 0.041) to test positive for DF IgG than those who did not routinely sleep under an ITN. title: Temporal Modeling of Weekly Dengue Cases in Marikina City: A Time-Respecting Comparison of Classical, Machine Learning, and Deep Temporal Models
abstract: Background Short-horizon dengue forecasting can support local preparedness, but model comparisons may be weakened by random splitting, information leakage, limited baseline testing, and insufficient out-of-time evaluation. This study developed a surveillance-only framework for forecasting weekly dengue incidence in Marikina City two weeks ahead. Methods Weekly records combined Marikina-filtered Department of Health–Epidemiology Bureau data from 2016–2020 with Marikina Epidemiology Surveillance Unit data from 2023–2025. The years 2021–2022 were excluded because the available records contained zero and three reported cases, respectively. Eight trained models—ARIMA, SARIMA, ETS, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, LSTM, and Temporal CNN—were compared with naïve and moving-average reference baselines. Target-year splits used 2024 for internal validation and model selection and 2025 as an out-of-time temporal holdout. Earlier observed 2025 case counts were permitted as causal inputs for forecasting later 2025 targets when they occurred before the relevant forecast origin. Mean absolute error was the primary metric, supported by root mean square error, coefficient of determination, feature importance, and incidence-class error analysis. Results The cleaned dataset contained 417 weekly observations and 8,263 reported cases. ARIMA was the strongest trained model during 2024 internal validation, although the two-week moving average and naïve baselines produced slightly lower errors. In the 2025 temporal holdout, LSTM achieved the most favorable metrics, with an MAE of 7.951, RMSE of 10.651, and R2 of 0.698, followed by ARIMA with an MAE of 8.652, RMSE of 11.686, and R2 of 0.636. Both achieved lower MAE than the naïve baseline. Tree-based models relied primarily on current incidence and two-week rolling summaries. All evaluated methods tended to underpredict outbreak-level weeks. Conclusions Surveillance-only forecasting was feasible under a leakage-safe temporal design. LSTM produced the strongest 2025 holdout metrics, while ARIMA remained an interpretable and computationally efficient alternative. Operational use should retain simple baselines, communicate uncertainty, and prioritize improved detection of rapid outbreak escalation.

Operational use should retain simple baselines, communicate uncertainty, and prioritize improved detection of rapid outbreak escalation. 1 BACKGROUND Dengue remains a persistent public health concern in tropical and subtropical settings, where seasonal increases can rapidly strain clinical services, vector-control operations, and local surveillance teams [1, 3]. In densely populated urban areas, short-term increases in reported cases can affect staffing, bed capacity, diagnostics, medical supplies, and the timing of community interventions. City-level forecasts are therefore Page 2/19 potentially more actionable than national or regional summaries because local government units make many operational decisions at the city and barangay levels. Routine dengue surveillance produces chronologically ordered counts that contain temporal dependence. Recent incidence may represent ongoing transmission chains, reporting momentum, and the early development of outbreak waves [15, 16]. Classical time-series models capture this dependence directly through autoregressive, moving-average, trend, and seasonal components [4, 8, 19]. Machine-learning approaches instead transform the series into lag, rolling, change, trend, and calendar predictors, while deep temporal models learn representations from ordered case sequences [11–14, 17]. Forecasting credibility depends as much on experimental design as on algorithm choice. Random train-test splits violate temporal order, and preprocessing performed before the forecast cutoff may leak future information into model inputs. Time-respecting validation, causal feature construction, and comparison with simple persistence baselines are necessary to determine whether a trained model offers genuine predictive value [5–7]. These safeguards are particularly important for weekly dengue data, where adjacent observations are strongly correlated and naive forecasts can be difficult to beat. Existing dengue studies have demonstrated the value of autoregressive methods, tree ensembles, and recurrent neural networks, but performance varies across locations, forecast horizons, covariates, and evaluation designs [5, 13, 17, 20]. Local surveillance agencies may also lack consistently available meteorological, mobility, socioeconomic, or environmental variables. A surveillance-only design based on case counts and reporting dates can therefore provide a practical, reproducible baseline for data-constrained settings, although it cannot explain causal transmission mechanisms. This study developed and evaluated a leakage-safe, two-week-ahead forecasting framework for weekly dengue incidence in Marikina City. The objectives were to: (1) characterize trend, seasonality, autocorrelation, and lag behavior; (2) compare classical, machine-learning, and deep temporal models; (3) determine whether trained models improve on naive and moving-average baselines; and (4) identify the temporal predictors most strongly used by tree-based models. The principal contribution is a complete target-year evaluation design with 2024 reserved for internal model development and 2025 retained as a full unseen external holdout. 2 METHODS 2.1 Study Design and Setting The study used a quantitative predictive design focused on weekly dengue incidence in Marikina City, Philippines. The task was univariate, two-week-ahead regression: information observed at forecast origin t was used to predict the weekly dengue case count at t + 2. The study evaluated predictive accuracy rather than causal effects. No individual-level or personally identifiable health records were analyzed. 2.2 Data Sources and Eligibility The unified dataset combined two surveillance sources. Department of Health-Epidemiology Bureau records were filtered to retain only Marikina City observations from 2016–2020 [2]. More recent weekly records for 2023–2025 were obtained from the Marikina Epidemiology Surveillance Unit (MESU). The available 2021 record Page 3/19 contained zero cases and the 2022 record contained only three cases; both years were excluded because they were too sparse to support reliable lag, rolling-window, and sequence modeling. The cleaned series contained 417 weekly records and 8,263 reported cases. The training and development period included 313 weeks from 2016–2020 and 2023, with 4,999 cases. The 2024 internal-validation year contained 52 weeks and 1,867 cases. The 2025 external holdout contained 52 weeks and 1,397 cases. All three sets had no remaining duplicate dates or missing case values. The 2025 holdout included 15 low, 14 moderate, 16 high, and seven very high or outbreak-level weeks, providing a broader test than a partial-year holdout. Table 1 summarizes the resulting dataset structure and data quality by period. Table 1 Dataset structure and data quality Period Years Weeks Cases Use Historical segment 1 2016–2020 261 3,468 Training/development Excluded interval 2021–2022 - 0 and 3 Excluded for insufficient reporting Historical segment 2 2023 52 1,531 Training/development Internal validation 2024 52 1,867 Model and hyperparameter selection External holdout 2025 52 1,397 Final unseen evaluation Note. The training/development total was 313 weeks and 4,999 cases. Dashes indicate that the excluded records were not treated as a modeling segment. 2.3 Data Preparation and Temporal Segmentation Dates were converted to a standard datetime representation, case counts were converted to numeric form, invalid dates and missing targets were removed, negative values were bounded at zero, and records were sorted chronologically. The median interval between observations was checked to verify reporting frequency; the uploaded unified dataset was already weekly, so no additional aggregation was applied. Outbreak peaks were retained because they represented epidemiologically meaningful events rather than errors. A gap longer than 21 days defined a new continuous segment. This prevented lags, rolling statistics, expanding seasonal means, and deep-learning sequences from crossing the excluded 2021–2022 interval. Consequently, the last observation in 2020 was not treated as immediately adjacent to the first observation in 2023. Classical- model input was handled differently: the available observations before each cutoff were chronologically concatenated without explicit missing calendar positions. This did not introduce future targets, but it may have affected estimates of autocorrelation and seasonality and is treated as a limitation. 2.4 Exploratory Temporal Analysis and Feature Engineering The autocorrelation function (ACF), partial autocorrelation function (PACF), monthly and weekly seasonal profiles, and Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess (STL) were used to examine short-range persistence and annual structure [4, 19]. Because the strongest dependence occurred at early lags and annual recurrence was irregular, the machine-learning feature set emphasized recent history rather than direct 26- or 52-week lags. Page 4/19 For Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting, each forecast origin included the current case count; lags at 1, 2, 4, 8, and 12 weeks; rolling means, sums, and standard deviations over 2, 4, 8, and 12 weeks; exponentially weighted means with spans of 4 and 8 weeks; one- and two-week differences; a bounded one- week percentage change; four- and eight-week local trend slopes; sine and cosine encodings of epidemiological week and month; a segment-local trend index; and expanding historical means for the same week and month. All transformations used only information available at or before the forecast origin. The supervised target was the case count two weeks later. LSTM and Temporal CNN inputs were constructed separately as segment-aware 12-week case sequences paired with the target at t + 2. ARIMA, SARIMA, and ETS operated on the chronological case-count series and did not use the engineered feature matrix. 2.5 Forecasting Models Five reference baselines were calculated without training: a naive forecast equal to the current observed case count and moving averages over the previous 2, 4, 8, and 12 weeks. Baselines were used only to establish the minimum practical standard and were not candidates for final trained-model selection. The classical models were ARIMA, SARIMA, and exponential smoothing (ETS). Candidate ARIMA orders (1,0,0), (2,0,0), and (3,0,0) were compared by 2024 rolling-origin MAE; ARIMA(3,0,0) was selected. SARIMA used order (1,0,0) with seasonal order (1,0,0,52). ETS used additive trend and additive seasonality with a 52-week period. ARIMA was repeatedly refitted at forecast origins, whereas SARIMA and ETS generated static full-horizon forecasts after fitting before the evaluation year [8–10]. The tree-based regressors were Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting. Candidate settings varied tree depth, leaf size, number of estimators, feature subsampling, learning rate, and subsampling ratio. Each candidate was evaluated with raw and log1p-transformed targets, and the configuration with the lowest 2024 MAE was selected. Random Forest reduces variance through bootstrap aggregation [11], while Gradient Boosting sequentially corrects residual error [12]. The LSTM used one recurrent layer with 32 hidden units followed by a linear output layer. The Temporal CNN used two one-dimensional convolutional layers with 32 channels per layer, kernel size 3, ReLU activations, adaptive average pooling, and a linear output. It is described as a Temporal CNN rather than a canonical dilated residual TCN because the implementation did not include explicit dilation or residual TCN blocks [14, 21]. Both neural models used training-derived standardization, Adam optimization with learning rate 0.001 and weight decay 0.0001, SmoothL1 loss, a maximum of 150 epochs, and early stopping with patience 12. Table 2 summarizes the input, selected configuration, and evaluation procedure for each trained model. Page 5/19 Table 2 Trained models and evaluation procedures Model Input and selected setup Evaluation procedure ARIMA Weekly series; selected order (3,0,0) Rolling-origin refitting in 2024 and 2025 SARIMA Weekly series; (1,0,0)(1,0,0,52) Static full-horizon forecast ETS Additive trend and seasonality; period 52 Static full-horizon forecast Decision Tree Engineered features; depth 3; leaf 5; log target Target-year validation and refit through 2024 Random Forest 200 trees; depth 5; max features 0.7; leaf 5 Target-year validation and refit through 2024 Gradient Boosting 100 trees; learning rate 0.05; depth 2 Target-year validation and refit through 2024 LSTM 12-week sequence; 32 hidden units Early stopping on 2024; final fit through 2024 Temporal CNN 12-week sequence; two Conv1D layers Early stopping on 2024; final fit through 2024 Note. Different forecast-generation procedures were retained by model family and are considered when interpreting direct comparisons. 2.6 Chronological Validation Observations were assigned according to the year of the forecast target rather than the year of the forecast origin. Targets occurring in 2023 or earlier formed the training and development set, targets occurring in 2024 formed the internal-validation set, and targets occurring in 2025 formed the out-of-time temporal holdout. This target-year assignment prevented forecasts originating near the end of one year from placing a target from the following year into an earlier split. The 2025 target values were excluded from ARIMA-order selection, machine-learning hyperparameter tuning, and initial neural-model validation. During the 2025 temporal holdout evaluation, earlier observed 2025 case counts could be used as historical inputs for later 2025 forecasts only when those observations occurred before the relevant forecast origin. Therefore, the 2025 targets remained held out from model development while forecasts were allowed to use causally available surveillance history. For the neural models, the 2024 validation period was used to select the architecture, training configuration, and number of training epochs. After these settings were fixed, the selected models were refitted using all eligible sequences through 2024 for the predetermined number of epochs without monitoring the 2025 holdout. The 2025 targets were then used only for final temporal evaluation. 2.7 Performance Measures and Interpretation Mean absolute error was treated as the primary operational metric because it directly represented the average weekly case-count error. Root mean square error was used to identify models with larger individual forecasting errors, while R2 provided supplementary information regarding variance explanation. Model conclusions were Page 6/19 based primarily on MAE and RMSE rather than on a custom percentage-accuracy measure. This evaluation approach follows established principles for assessing point forecasts using proper scoring rules [18]. Native impurity-based feature importance was extracted from the selected tree-based models. These scores describe how strongly predictors were used within each fitted model but do not represent causal relationships or permutation-based importance. Errors during the 2025 temporal holdout were also summarized according to incidence level. All analyses were performed in Python using pandas and NumPy for data handling, statsmodels for classical models, scikit-learn for tree regressors and evaluation, and PyTorch for neural models. Fixed random seeds and explicit configurations were used where supported. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Data Characteristics and Temporal Structure Annual totals varied substantially. The highest observed total was 1,867 cases in 2024, followed by 1,531 in 2023 and 1,397 in 2025. Weekly incidence included low-transmission periods and abrupt peaks, indicating that the series was not governed by a uniform annual trajectory. The feature-generation process produced 292 model-ready supervised observations: 189 with targets through 2023, 51 for 2024, and 52 for 2025. The deep- learning sequence dataset retained 52 targets in each evaluation year. Figure 1 shows the resulting weekly incidence series. Figure description: A weekly line plot covering 2016–2020 and 2023–2025 shows several irregular peaks, a gap for excluded 2021–2022 data, high activity in 2023–2024, and a lower but still variable full-year pattern in 2025. The ACF showed strong positive dependence at early lags, declining gradually across the following weeks. The PACF concentrated its strongest direct effects at lags 1 and 2. A weaker secondary ACF rise appeared near the annual range, but it was less pronounced than short-range persistence. These findings supported the reduced lag set and the emphasis on current incidence and rolling summaries. Figure 2 presents the ACF and PACF diagnostics described above. title_zh: 马里基纳市每周登革热病例的时间建模:经典、机器学习和深度时间模型的时间尊重比较
source_body_en: Background Short-horizon dengue forecasting can support local preparedness, but model comparisons may be weakened by random splitting, information leakage, limited baseline testing, and insufficient out-of-time evaluation. This study developed a surveillance-only framework for forecasting weekly dengue incidence in Marikina City two weeks ahead. Methods Weekly records combined Marikina-filtered Department of Health–Epidemiology Bureau data from 2016–2020 with Marikina Epidemiology Surveillance Unit data from 2023–2025. The years 2021–2022 were excluded because the available records contained zero and three reported cases, respectively. Eight trained models—ARIMA, SARIMA, ETS, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, LSTM, and Temporal CNN—were compared with naïve and moving-average reference baselines. Target-year splits used 2024 for internal validation and model selection and 2025 as an out-of-time temporal holdout. Earlier observed 2025 case counts were permitted as causal inputs for forecasting later 2025 targets when they occurred before the relevant forecast origin. Mean absolute error was the primary metric, supported by root mean square error, coefficient of determination, feature importance, and incidence-class error analysis. Results The cleaned dataset contained 417 weekly observations and 8,263 reported cases. ARIMA was the strongest trained model during 2024 internal validation, although the two-week moving average and naïve baselines produced slightly lower errors. In the 2025 temporal holdout, LSTM achieved the most favorable metrics, with an MAE of 7.951, RMSE of 10.651, and R2 of 0.698, followed by ARIMA with an MAE of 8.652, RMSE of 11.686, and R2 of 0.636. Both achieved lower MAE than the naïve baseline. Tree-based models relied primarily on current incidence and two-week rolling summaries. All evaluated methods tended to underpredict outbreak-level weeks. Conclusions Surveillance-only forecasting was feasible under a leakage-safe temporal design. LSTM produced the strongest 2025 holdout metrics, while ARIMA remained an interpretable and computationally efficient alternative. Operational use should retain simple baselines, communicate uncertainty, and prioritize improved detection of rapid outbreak escalation.
abstract_zh: 背景 短期登革热预报可以支持当地的准备工作,但模型比较可能会因随机分裂、信息泄漏、有限的基线测试和不充分的过时评估而受到削弱。这项研究开发了一个仅 监测 的框架,用于预测马里基纳市未来两周的每周登革热 监测。方法 每周记录将 2016-2020 年经马里基纳过滤的卫生部 –流行病学 局数据与 2023-2025 年马里基纳 流行病学 监测 单位数据相结合。2021-2022 年被排除在外,因为现有记录分别包含 0 例和 3 例报告病例。将八种经过训练的模型(ARIMA、SARIMA、ETS、决策树、随机森林、梯度提升、LSTM 和时态 CNN)与朴素参考基线和移动平均参考基线进行了比较。目标年份划分使用 2024 年进行内部验证和模型选择,并使用 2025 年作为不合时宜的时间保留。当早期观察到的 2025 年病例数发生在相关预测原点之前时,允许将其作为预测 2025 年后期目标的因果输入。平均绝对误差是主要指标,由均方根误差、确定系数、特征重要性和 发病率 类误差分析支持。结果 清理后的数据集包含 417 个每周观察值和 8,263 个报告病例。尽管两周移动平均值和朴素基线产生的误差略低,但 ARIMA 是 2024 年内部验证期间训练最强的模型。在 2025 年的时间保留中,LSTM 实现了最有利的指标,MAE 为 7.951,RMSE 为 10.651,R2 为 0.698,其次是 ARIMA,MAE 为 8.652,RMSE 为 11.686,R2 为 0.636。两者的 MAE 均低于初始基线。基于树的模型主要依赖于当前的 发病率 和两周滚动摘要。所有评估的方法都倾向于低估 暴发 级别的周数。结论 在泄漏安全时间设计下,仅 监测 预测是可行的。LSTM 产生了最强的 2025 年保留指标,而 ARIMA 仍然是一个可解释且计算效率高的替代方案。操作使用应保留简单的基线,传达不确定性,并优先改进对 暴发 快速升级的检测。
